summary: Proposes a program to develop a directory service for the Internet. It reports results of a meeting in February 1989 convened to review requirements and options. It is offered for comment and not as a committed research activity.

eli5.summary: People wanted an Internet phone book to find other people and things. This is a plan, from a meeting, about how to start building one.

subtitle: A roadmap for building a unified Internet-wide directory service.

tldr.problem: The expanding Internet needed a unified way to find people's email addresses and other network information, but different organizations were building incompatible directory systems.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes a three-stage approach: field trials comparing X.500 and alternative directory services, production implementation of the best approach, and full deployment with proper data management and authority delegation.
tldr.outcome: This plan established the framework for Internet directory service development, with X.500 chosen as the foundation standard. Though the ambitious three-year timeline was not met, it influenced directory service work for decades.

facts.label: Estimated user base
facts.value: 10 million across tens of thousands of organizations

facts.label: Expected query rate
facts.value: 170 queries per second average, 100 million per week

facts.label: Timeline to deployment
facts.value: 3 years from field trials to full deployment

today: RFC 1107 is Informational and was never obsoleted, standing as a historical record of the 1989 consensus on Internet directory service planning. The technical recommendations were never officially adopted as a standard, but the three-stage approach and selection of X.500 influenced directory service work for years. LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol, RFC 3377 and successors) eventually provided a practical implementation path for X.500-based directories on the Internet.

sections.title: The Need for a White Pages Service
sections.content:
As the Internet expanded from computer scientists to support the broader scientific research community, researchers needed a way to locate colleagues and their network resources. Email was becoming common, but users had to know exact addresses or check local directories. The RFC calls for a white pages service (like a telephone directory for the Internet) where anyone could search by name to find email addresses, phone numbers, or other information about people and computers.

Several partial solutions already existed: the Domain Name System (DNS) for machines, Xerox Clearinghouse for directory services, DEC's naming service (DNANS), and experimental systems like Profile. However, these systems had different designs and could not interwork. In February 1989, a meeting of experts from academic, commercial, and government sectors reached consensus on how to proceed: build on the emerging X.500 international standard while evaluating alternative approaches.
sections.eli5: Email was growing, and people needed to find each other's addresses. Different organizations had different phone books that didn't work together, so experts met to plan one unified system for everyone.

sections.title: Requirements for a White Pages Service
sections.content:
The RFC identifies critical requirements. The service must handle approximately 100 million queries per week (roughly 170 per second on average) from an estimated 10 million users across tens of thousands of organizations. This demands a distributed system with multiple servers to avoid bottlenecks. Response time must be acceptable to users—ideally one second for a simple lookup, at most ten seconds.

Because the service would span many organizations, each needing control over their own data, the system must support partitioned authority: each organization delegates authority over its portion of the directory, similar to how domain delegation works in DNS. The service must also enforce access control, allowing some organizations to restrict personnel information visibility, and support multiple underlying network protocols (TCP/IP, DECnet, OSI) since organizations used different network stacks in 1989.
sections.eli5: The phone book needed to be super fast, handle millions of people from many organizations, let each organization control their own entries, and work with different computer networks.

sections.title: Comparing Directory Service Approaches
sections.content:
The RFC examines four main candidates. DNS, already widely deployed and proven scalable, was designed for hostnames but could be extended. Clearinghouse, used by Xerox worldwide, had proven experience managing scale and updates. DNANS, part of the DECnet architecture, excelled at access control, replication, and caching—features X.500 did not yet provide. Profile, an experimental system from the University of Arizona, supported sophisticated attribute-based searching and non-hierarchical naming rather than a strict tree structure.

X.500, the emerging CCITT (now ITU) international standard, offered rich semantics, hierarchical structure, and attribute-based search with filters. However, X.500 was incomplete: it said nothing about access control, replication, caching, data management tools, or how to organize the directory hierarchy. The consensus was that X.500 would become the standard others would adopt, making it the right foundation even though it needed additional work.
sections.eli5: Different systems had different strengths: DNS was fast and simple, Xerox's system had good management, DEC's system had good access control, and a university system allowed flexible searching. X.500 would become the international standard, so it was chosen even though it needed improvement.

sections.title: The Three-Stage Implementation Plan
sections.content:
Stage 1 (Field Trials), planned for one year, would test X.500, Profile, and DNANS in controlled environments (primarily computer science departments). The goal was to distinguish problems inherent to X.500's specification from artifacts of particular implementations, and to learn which approaches best addressed issues X.500 did not cover. The trials would also compare at least two X.500 implementations to separate specification issues from implementation artifacts. Key projects included modifying services to use a common data format and developing user interfaces and data-gathering tools.

Stage 2 (Implementation), planned for the second and third years, would produce production-quality code for whichever approach the field trials validated. This included building multiple user interface clients for different computers and skill levels, from novices doing simple lookups to advanced users performing complex searches. Stage 3 (Deployment), planned for completion in three years total, would involve gathering user data, placing servers, training users, and managing the growing service. Deployment planning would begin during Stage 1 so information collection could start early.
sections.eli5: The plan had three parts: test different systems in colleges for one year to learn what works best; spend two years building production code; then spend three years spreading it to the Internet and filling it with real data.

sections.title: Conclusion and Legacy
sections.content:
The RFC concludes with consensus that pursuing X.500 was both correct and feasible, while acknowledging that X.500 needed elaboration in several areas. The participants recognized that interoperability with X.500 would become necessary as other parts of the networked world adopted it, making it the pragmatic choice despite its limitations. The participants also emphasized that speed in implementation was crucial—acting immediately would establish a unified solution before a proliferation of incompatible directory services emerged.

Though the specific three-stage timeline proposed was ambitious and ultimately not met as planned, this RFC laid important groundwork for directory service development in the Internet community. The requirements and trade-offs identified here remained central to directory service design for decades. X.500 and its descendants, especially LDAP (Lightweight Directory Access Protocol), eventually became standard in many sectors.
sections.eli5: The experts agreed X.500 was the right choice because other networks were already using it, and the Internet needed to act fast to build one system before everyone built their own incompatible versions.
